lessons.title: Case Study: Nifty FMCG vs Nifty Metal Through the 2020 Crash and Recovery

body.text: In the 2020 crash, Nifty FMCG fell about half as much as Nifty Metal and recovered its old high four months sooner. Then, over the next 21 months, metals rose more than four times as much. Defensives win the fall. Cyclicals win the rebound. Almost nobody catches both by switching.

children.text: Chapter 2 followed a cyclical company's earnings through a full cycle. This case study follows prices. The 2020 pandemic gave Indian markets the fastest crash and one of the sharpest recoveries in their history, which makes it a clean test of everything in this chapter: how defensives and cyclicals behave when fear peaks, when hope returns, and when the cycle turns again. All figures below are daily closing levels of the NSE's Nifty FMCG, Nifty Metal, and Nifty 50 indices.

body.title: Month-End Closes Indexed to 100 at End of January 2020

children.text: Phase 1: The Crash, Where Defensives Earned Their Premium

Everything fell, which is exactly what Chapter 1 warned: in a panic, share prices do not separate cleanly by business quality. But the size of the falls lined up with the spectrum. FMCG, the true defensive, fell 26.3%. The Nifty 50, a blend, fell 38.4%. Metal, the deep cyclical, fell 48.8%. By 30 June 2020, Nifty FMCG was only 4.5% below its January peak, while Nifty Metal was still 31.8% below.

body.caption: A fall of 50% needs a 100% gain to get back to where it started

body.title: The Climb Back
body.prompt: Nifty Metal fell from 2,921.45 to 1,496.45. By what percentage did it need to rise from that low just to get back to its January 2020 peak? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: 2,921.45 ÷ 1,496.45 = 1.952, so the index needed to rise about 95.2%. Nifty FMCG, which fell only 26.3%, needed about 35.8% to recover, and the Nifty 50 needed about 62.4%. Smaller falls need much smaller recoveries, which is why FMCG was back at its high by July 2020 while metals took until late November.

children.text: Phase 2: The Recovery, Where Cyclicals Took Over

Once the worst fear passed, the order flipped completely. Global stimulus, supply shortages, and reopening demand sent metal prices soaring, and metal companies' earnings exploded, as Tata Steel's jump from ₹8,190 crore in FY21 to ₹41,749 crore in FY22 showed in Chapter 2. FMCG earnings kept growing steadily, but steady growth could not compete with an earnings boom.

cells: Still below January peak on 30 June 2020
Whole period: January 2020 peak to 30 December 2022

body.text: Look at the timing. Nifty Metal bottomed on 23 March 2020 and was already up 117.5% from that low by 31 December 2020, while metal companies were still reporting weak profits for FY20 and the early part of FY21. The market priced in the earnings recovery many months before it appeared in results. Then Nifty Metal peaked in October 2021, before those same companies reported their record FY22 profits. Cyclical stocks turn ahead of cyclical earnings, in both directions.

body.title: Why Did Metals Rally So Early?
body.question: By December 2020, Nifty Metal was more than double its March 2020 low, even though most metal companies had not yet reported strong profits. What best explains this?
options: Metal stocks are defensive, so they always recover first
Investors were pricing in the expected surge in metal prices and future earnings as economies reopened
Metal companies' reported earnings had already hit records by March 2020
The Nifty Metal index changed its constituents
body.explanation: Share prices discount expected future earnings. As stimulus and reopening pushed global metal prices up, investors bought ahead of the earnings boom that showed up in FY22 results. This is why waiting for strong reported earnings before buying a cyclical usually means buying late.

children.text: Phase 3: The Turn, Where Defensives Protected Again

In the first half of 2022, inflation surged, central banks including the RBI began raising rates, and metal prices cooled. The steel export duty from 22 May added pressure. From 31 December 2021 to 30 June 2022, Nifty Metal fell 15.6% and the Nifty 50 fell 9.1%, while Nifty FMCG ended essentially flat. The defensive pattern reappeared as soon as the cycle turned down.

body.title: What Each Group Did for Investors

columns.label: Nifty FMCG (defensive)
points: First to regain its high, by July 2020
Held flat in the first half of 2022 downturn
Lagged badly in the recovery: +62.1% from the low versus +269.0% for metals

columns.label: Nifty Metal (cyclical)
points: Last to regain its high, in late November 2020
Fell hardest again in the first half of 2022
Biggest overall winner: +130.1% from the January 2020 peak to December 2022

body.title: The Switch That Cost Twice
body.scenario: Vikram held a Nifty Metal index fund in January 2020. In late March 2020, down almost 50%, he panicked and switched everything into an FMCG fund, reasoning that defensives were safer. In early 2022, watching metal stocks' huge gains, he switched back into metals just before the first-half 2022 slump.
body.prompt: Using the phase table, describe what Vikram's switches did to his returns, and what a better approach would have been.
body.modelAnswer: Vikram sold metals at close to the bottom, locking in a loss of nearly 50%, and bought FMCG, which rose about 62% from the March low to December 2021 while metals rose about 269%. He missed most of the cyclical recovery. He then bought metals back after the rally, around the end of 2021, and caught a 15.6% fall in the first half of 2022 while FMCG was flat. Each switch followed recent performance, so he owned defensives when cyclicals led and cyclicals when defensives protected. A better approach is to decide the defensive and cyclical mix in advance, based on risk tolerance and time horizon, and rebalance back to that mix periodically. Rebalancing would have made him buy metals after the crash, when they were cheap, and trim them after the rally, the opposite of what fear and greed made him do.

body.text: Sector indices have concentrated holdings. Nifty FMCG is heavily weighted towards a handful of large stocks such as ITC and Hindustan Unilever, and Nifty Metal towards the largest steel, aluminium, and mining companies. A single company's news can move the whole index, so check an index's current constituents and weights on the NSE indices website before treating it as a pure proxy for a sector.

body.title: Replicate This Study for the Next Downturn
steps: Download daily historical data for Nifty FMCG, Nifty Metal, and Nifty 50 from the NSE indices website
Identify the pre-fall peak close and the lowest close for each index
Calculate the fall for each and the gain needed to recover
Record the date each index regains its prior peak
Measure performance from the low over the following 12 and 24 months
Compare with reported earnings for leading companies in each index over the same period
Note what you would have done with a fixed allocation and periodic rebalancing versus switching based on recent performance
